explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Verse 31 says, “When the LORD saw that Leah was unloved, He opened her womb…” Leah is Jacob's wife, the one he loves less than her sister. The LORD saw her, and then He acted. I think that's worth slowing down for.

explanations.answer: He gives her flocks of her own
explanations.explanation: No flocks for Leah in this verse, friend. What the text says is that the LORD opened her womb. Sheep would have been a fine gift, but it isn't the one this verse gives. Leah's story here is about children.

explanations.answer: He sends her back to her father
explanations.explanation: Nobody's packing Leah's bags, friend. Verse 31 says, “When the LORD saw that Leah was unloved, He opened her womb…” He saw her first, and then He acted. I think that's the part worth holding onto.

Not quite, friend. Verse 31 ends with “but Rachel was barren.” Rachel is Leah's sister and the wife Jacob loves more. While Leah's family starts growing, Rachel's side stays empty. I think that sets up everything that comes next.
Right, baker. Genesis 29:31 says plainly, “but Rachel was barren.” Rachel is Leah's sister and the wife Jacob loves more. So Leah is the one with babies on the way, and Rachel is the one waiting.

Yes, love. Leah says, “The LORD has seen my affliction. Surely my husband will love me now.” She is hoping a baby boy changes how Jacob feels about her. You can hear how much she wants it in that one little word, “surely.”
Thanks is a nice idea, but it isn't what Leah says. After naming Reuben, she says, “Surely my husband will love me now.” What she's hoping for is Jacob's love. Quite a bit more than a thank-you card.

Trust isn't the word she picks, friend. Leah says, “The LORD has seen my affliction. Surely my husband will love me now.” Love is what she hopes Reuben will bring her. Think of her hope as a whole batch riding on one little boy.

That's right. Leah says, “Because the LORD has heard that I am unloved, He has given me this son as well.” Then she names him Simeon. The first time she said the LORD had seen her. This time she says He has heard her. I think that's a lot to carry, and she says it out loud.

Close, but the text says otherwise, baker. In Genesis 29:33 Leah says, “Because the LORD has heard that I am unloved, He has given me this son as well.” That's when she names him Simeon. So the LORD has heard her, and she says so.

explanations.answer: This time I will praise the LORD
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. When Judah is born, Leah says, “This time I will praise the LORD.” With Levi she spoke about her husband becoming attached to her (Genesis 29:34). With Judah she says she will praise the LORD, and I think that's worth noticing.

explanations.answer: This time I will ask for a daughter
explanations.explanation: No asking for a daughter here, friend. Leah says, “This time I will praise the LORD.” A daughter, Dinah, does come later, in Genesis 30:21. But that's a different verse, and Leah never says she asked for her.

explanations.answer: This time my husband will stay with me
explanations.explanation: That sounds like her earlier lines, so I get it. After Levi she says her husband will become attached to her (Genesis 29:34). With Judah, though, she says, “This time I will praise the LORD.” Her words turn toward the LORD, and I think that's the whole point of this one.

Not this time, baker. The very next line says, “Then Leah stopped having children.” Judah makes four sons, and then the baby parade stops. I think it's a lovely place to pause, since Leah names him with “This time I will praise the LORD.”

You got it, baker. After Judah, the text says, “Then Leah stopped having children.” Four sons, and the baby parade takes a break. Her last words at that birth were “This time I will praise the LORD.” and I think that's a good note to stop on.

explanations.answer: Give me children or I will die
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The text says Rachel envied her sister, and then she says to Jacob, “Give me children, or I will die!” No hints and no warm-up, just straight to the point. I think Jacob felt that one.

explanations.answer: Pray to the LORD for me
explanations.explanation: That would be a quieter request, friend, but it isn't what the text has. Rachel says, “Give me children, or I will die!” She says it straight to Jacob. Praying isn't in her words here.

Sending Leah away isn't what Rachel asks for, friend. The text says she envied her sister, and then she tells Jacob, “Give me children, or I will die!” Her request is about children. Envy is the feeling the text names.
Yes, God. Jacob asks, “Am I in the place of God, who has withheld children from you?” Jacob is angry when he says it. He points past himself to the One who gives children.

Laban, Rachel's father (Genesis 29:16), doesn't come up in Jacob's answer. Jacob asks, “Am I in the place of God, who has withheld children from you?” He's speaking about God. Laban isn't in this conversation at all.

Leah's name never comes up in Jacob's answer, friend. Rachel has just spoken to him, and he says, “Am I in the place of God, who has withheld children from you?” The word he lands on is God. I think that was a tense moment between those two.

explanations.answer: So Bilhah can bear children for her
explanations.explanation: That's right. Rachel says, “Here is my maidservant Bilhah. Sleep with her, that she may bear children for me, so that through her I too can build a family.” Bilhah is Rachel's servant. Rachel's goal is to have children through her. This is a heavy part of the story, so we'll just let the text speak.

explanations.answer: So Bilhah can serve Leah instead
explanations.explanation: Leah doesn't come into Rachel's plan, friend. Rachel says Bilhah is to bear children for her, “…so that through her I too can build a family.” Bilhah is Rachel's servant. Nothing in the verse moves her over to Leah.

explanations.answer: So Bilhah can care for the flocks
explanations.explanation: Sheep aren't what Rachel is thinking about here. She tells Jacob that Bilhah, her servant, may “…bear children for me, so that through her I too can build a family.” That's the plan in her own words. Flocks never come up in this part of the story.

That's not what the text says, baker. Genesis 30:4 says Rachel gave Jacob her servant Bilhah as a wife, and he slept with her. Verse 5 says Bilhah conceived and bore him a son. So Jacob goes along with it.

Right. Jacob doesn't refuse. Genesis 30:4 says Rachel gave Bilhah to Jacob as a wife, “…and he slept with her…” Then Bilhah conceives and bears a son. The text doesn't say what Jacob was thinking, and I won't guess.

That's it, baker. Rachel says, “In my great struggles, I have wrestled with my sister and won.” Leah is the sister. Naphtali is the name Rachel gives this second son of Bilhah. Rachel picks a wrestling match for her words, and she calls it a win.
Her father isn't who she says she wrestled. Rachel says, “In my great struggles, I have wrestled with my sister and won.” Her sister is Leah. The struggle is between the two of them.

Rachel does have words with Jacob earlier, but that's not this line. Here she says, “In my great struggles, I have wrestled with my sister and won.” Her sister is Leah. This is how she names Naphtali, and Jacob isn't the one she's wrestling.

explanations.answer: She gives Jacob her servant Zilpah
explanations.explanation: You got it. Genesis 30:9 says Leah saw that she had stopped having children, so she gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob as a wife. Zilpah is Leah's servant. Rachel did something similar with Bilhah, and now Leah does her own version of it.

explanations.answer: She asks Rachel to share Bilhah
explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but Leah doesn't ask Rachel for anything here. Bilhah is Rachel's servant, and Leah has a servant of her own. Genesis 30:9 says Leah saw that she had stopped having children, so she gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob as a wife. Leah makes this move on her own.

explanations.answer: She sends Jacob back to Rachel
explanations.explanation: Leah waving Jacob off toward Rachel? Not in this verse, baker. Genesis 30:9 says she saw that she had stopped having children, so she gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob as a wife. I think Leah isn't ready to sit this one out.
That's right. Leah says, “How happy I am! For the women call me happy.” She names this son Asher. Happy is the word she picks, and she says it twice in one breath. Let's let her enjoy it.

Foolish? Not in this verse, friend. Leah says, “How happy I am! For the women call me happy.” Zilpah bore the son, and Leah is the one who names him Asher. Happy is the word she picks, so let's let her enjoy it.
Nobody is talking money in this verse, baker. Leah says, “How happy I am! For the women call me happy.” That's why she names him Asher. Happy is the word, and it's already worth plenty.

Not quite, baker. Genesis 30:14 says Reuben found mandrakes in the field during the wheat harvest and brought them to his mother. His mother is Leah, so the mandrakes go to Leah first. Rachel is the one who then asks Leah for some.

You got it, friend. Reuben finds mandrakes in the field during the wheat harvest and brings them to his mother, Leah. Rachel, his aunt, doesn't get them delivered. She has to ask, and she begs Leah, “Please give me some of your son’s mandrakes.”

That's the word. Leah says, “Is it not enough that you have taken away my husband?” She says it to Rachel, her sister. That's a pointed thing to say. I think there's a lot of hurt sitting behind that one question.

Her father isn't what she's upset about here. Leah says, “Is it not enough that you have taken away my husband? Now you want to take my son’s mandrakes as well?” Husband is the word she uses. Her father isn't part of this exchange.

Sheep never come up in this argument, friend. Leah says, “Is it not enough that you have taken away my husband?” Her husband, Jacob, is what she names. The mandrakes are the only thing in the field she mentions.

That's what Rachel offers. In Genesis 30:15 she says, “he may sleep with you tonight in exchange for your son’s mandrakes.” The “he” is Jacob, so the trade is a night with him for the mandrakes. Leah had just asked, “Is it not enough that you have taken away my husband?” I think this one is a tense trade.

Bilhah, Rachel's servant, was already part of Rachel's plan earlier in the passage. She isn't what Rachel offers here. Rachel says, “he may sleep with you tonight in exchange for your son’s mandrakes.” The deal is about a night with Jacob.

No sheep change hands in this deal, baker. Rachel says, “he may sleep with you tonight in exchange for your son’s mandrakes.” The trade is a night with Jacob for the mandrakes. Sheep never come up in this conversation.

She keeps going, baker. Genesis 30:17 says, “And God listened to Leah, and she conceived and bore a fifth son to Jacob.” Then she has a sixth son, and after that a daughter. So her family keeps growing.

Right. Genesis 30:17 says, “And God listened to Leah, and she conceived and bore a fifth son to Jacob.” That's Issachar, so after that night Leah does have another son. A sixth son comes after him, and then a daughter. Her family keeps growing, baker.

explanations.answer: Giving her maidservant to her husband
explanations.explanation: That's it. Leah says, “God has rewarded me for giving my maidservant to my husband.” Her maidservant is Zilpah. She says it as she names her fifth son, Issachar.

explanations.answer: Finding the mandrakes in the field
explanations.explanation: Reuben is the one who found the mandrakes, baker, not Leah. What she says is, “God has rewarded me for giving my maidservant to my husband.” The mandrakes are part of the story, but they aren't her reason here.

Leah did say she would praise the LORD when Judah was born (Genesis 29:35). But that's not what she says here, friend. She says, “God has rewarded me for giving my maidservant to my husband.” Praising every morning isn't in her words.

You've got it, baker. Genesis 30:22 says, “Then God remembered Rachel. He listened to her and opened her womb…” After all that waiting, God acts. The verse is plain, and I think it's one of the sweetest lines in this passage.

The text says otherwise, friend. Genesis 30:22 says, “Then God remembered Rachel. He listened to her and opened her womb…” Rachel has been waiting a long time in this story. In this verse, God opens her womb.
That's the word, baker. Rachel says, “God has taken away my shame…” She says it when her son is born. She gives credit to God, and the text lets her say it in her own words.

Fear isn't the word she picks, friend. Rachel says, “God has taken away my shame…” Earlier she told Jacob, “Give me children, or I will die!” (Genesis 30:1). But at the birth, shame is what she names.
Envy shows up earlier in the story, since Genesis 30:1 says Rachel envied her sister. But that isn't what she says at this birth. Here she says, “God has taken away my shame…” The word is shame.

explanations.answer: May the LORD add to me another son
explanations.explanation: That's right. In the same verse where she names Joseph, Rachel says, “May the LORD add to me another son.” Her words right after his name are a request for one more boy. I think that's hope, baker.

explanations.answer: May the LORD give me a daughter
explanations.explanation: A daughter isn't what Rachel asks for. After naming Joseph, she says, “May the LORD add to me another son.” The word is son. The only daughter named in this passage is Dinah, and she's Leah's (Genesis 30:21).

explanations.answer: May the LORD bless my sister too
explanations.explanation: That's a kind thought, but it isn't what the verse says, friend. Rachel says, “May the LORD add to me another son.” Her words are about her own family. Leah isn't mentioned in this line.
